content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors tackle noisy label learning with a causality perspective. They assume the causal relations are in the format of the DAG in Fig. 2(c). Under this assumption, they propose a method to deconfound the spurious correlation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The authors tackle noisy label learning with a new perspective. The generating process in Fig. 2(c) is sensible. However, there are many faults. And the writing can be improved largely. Many important details are missing. I list them in the next part.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. I suggest the authors show the relations between $Y',Z_f,Y,Z_b,L$ in a graph. The authors said Y' is a confounder between Z_f and Y. Does Y' have a causal relation to Y? Why?

2. In Fig. 2(c), there is a directed edge from $Y'$ to $Z_b$, the authors said it is because the noisy labels supervise the network to update its parameters. According to this explanation, why is not a directed edge from $Y$ to $Z_b$ in Fig. 2 (b)? In other words, why is "When the label is clean, the network tends to focus on the right foreground and the background features are close to a random variable. Otherwise when the label is noisy, the network tends to focus on the background and thus id-irrelevant background details are learnt".

3. Line 3 of Eq. 2, It seems to be $p(y'|b)$ in the denominator ( $p(f|b)=\int_{y'}p(y'|b)p(f|b,y')$ )

4. It is unclear what Eq. 2 implies. For the Eq. 2.b, if we put the $P(L|f,b)$ on the right hand out of the fraction, the whole equation is just $P(L|Z_f=f,Z_b=b)= 1 * P(L|Z_f=f,Z_b=b)$. Does it has any physical meaning?

5. On Eq. 3, there is $Y$ on the left. Where is it on the right? Or should it be $L$?

6. The induction of Eq. 3 also seems wrong. The probability term $p(y'|b)$ is a conditional probability. Why is it related to do operation? $p(y'|do(b))$ equals to $p(y')$, but $p(y'|b)$ does not.
content.summary_of_the_review: I give a negative score because the mathematical derivation seems not correct and some details are unclear. I am happy to change my score if my questions are addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper tackles the problem of improving learning from noisy labels by introducing the concept of adaptive disentanglement of foreground from background, thus eliminating the spurious correlation between labels and background representation and preserving true causal effect between labels and foreground representation. 
The paper provides an extensive experimentation withe very impressive results for both synthetic and real noise datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The paper comes up with a very ***interesting idea*** -- noisy labels make the network associate background features to the label, creating spurious correlations and eventually hurting the performance, so we need to remove the influence of the background features, to avoid noise influence. The paper further proposes a method to implement such a disentanglement.  
2) The paper shows the effectiveness of the idea by extensive experiments, achieving 0.5-2% improvement on synthetic data   (Tables 1 and 2) and almost 1% improvement for real world noise (Table 3) 

Weaknesses:
1) The paper provides somewhat superficial motivation (not supported by extensive experimentation - only Figure1, which is not very clear).
2) The paper is not very clear, has many English typos and errors, and does not provide a clear implementation strategy 
3) The results on Clothing1M do not achieved SOTA (Table 5), which might mean: (1) The idea only works for very specific datasets where the classification task is mostly about the foreground object; (2) issue with implementation  --- it would be great if the authors can suggest their explanation
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is mostly clear, apart from the most important part of implementation.   

Quality:
English quality can be improved :
Below I ***highlighted*** several examples from the last paragraph of Section 3.1 (there are many more examples in the paper): 
where Zf and Zb are the representations of foreground and background, η denotes the noise, m1 (⋅, ⋅) and m2 (⋅, ⋅, ⋅)  ***demotes***  the unknown ***structual***  functions. Note that every variable here are a random variable with a certain distribution. The noise η is independent of the representation. And given the clean unknown label Y , the foreground feature Zf is is independent of noisy label Y ′. F indicates the noise distribution.
Although the function m2(⋅) has better properties of independence, in the noisy labels setting, the clean label Y is unknown, and in our setting, the noisy distribution F is also unknown, which further ***make*** the estimation of m(⋅) intractable. 

The paper can be revised to remove duplicate parts (like second paragraph of introduction and second paragraph of Section 3.1)

Novelty: To the best of my knowledge the idea is novel in the domain of learning from noisy labels 

Reproducibility: Unfortunately the code is not provided and the suggested approach cannot be easily implemented from the provided equations.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In overall I have mixed feelings about the paper. The idea is interesting and relatively novel in the field of noisy label training, the empirical results are also impressive. However, the lack of clarity of the paper and lack of more thoughtful motivation  make me hesitant to support this paper with accept. 
I would love to read a revision and decide accordingly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a causal approach to overcome malignant bias due to spurious correlation between background and label in object recognition.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
PRO
- Addresses a critical problem for real-world applications
- A causal perspective seems sensible in this setting

CONs:
- Poorly organized, causal intervention not well explained

- The method does not address the general problem of noisy labels (as
  other approaches dealing with noisy labeling), but addresses a
  specific setting (object recognition) and a specific type of noise
  ((spurious correlation between image background and label)

- More than dealing with noisy labels, the authors seem to address the
  (or one instance of the) problem of confounders in learning. There
  is a large body of literature dealing with this problem (see e.g.
  Qingyu Zhao, Ehsan Adeli, and Kilian M Pohl. Training
  confounder-free deep learning models for medical
  applications. Nature Communications, 2020.), especially when the
  confounder is the background as is the case here. The authors
  completely overlooked this literature, which is the most appropriate
  for an empirical comparison.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is poorly organized. The introduction + related work are
very long with a lot of repetitions. This leaves little room for the
description of the approach, and equations 1 and especially 2 are
poorly presented (btw, Zb indep Y' | Y in eq. 1, I guess Zb should be Zf).

Minor: you need to distinguish between cite and citep.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My main concern with this work, apart from a certain lack of clarity,
is that it should be framed in the area of learning unbiased
predictions, which is very active with a plethora of different
approaches, especially for dealing with bias coming from the
background.  The novelty and advantage of the proposed solution with
respect to the SOTA in this area is not investigated.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of noisy labels learning from a causal-effect view. The paper proposed a deconfounded noisy labels learning method, DeNLL. The proposed DeNLL method includes a localization module adaptively determining the foreground from the background and a debiased interaction module encouraging the mutual information exchange between the debiased factor and original representations. By extensive experiments on five popular benchmarks, the paper validates that DeNLL achieves the state- of-the-art performances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
(1) The paper solves an important problem from a novel perspective.
(2) The paper validates the proposed method by extensive experiments, including multiple datasets and baselines.
(3) The paper is well written and easy to read.

Weaknesses:
(1) The paper claims that `for the first time, the problem of noisy labels learning is studied from a causal-effect view.' However, there are some existing works, such as

Yao, Yu, et al. "Instance-dependent label-noise learning under a structural causal model." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 4409-4420.
Wu, Songhua, et al. "Fair classification with instance-dependent label noise." Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning. PMLR, 2022.

The paper may be better positioned, by discussing the relation between this work and related works.

(2) The paper seems to make strong assumptions that (i) the background and foreground is well defined and accurately known to the model and (ii) the confounders (in the proposed causal graph) are only from the background. However, in real-world images, the task can be more complex. For example, in images with complex scenes and multiple objects, the background and foreground may not be well-defined. And one object can be the confounder, when inference on the other object, e.g., as in

Wang, Tan, et al. "Visual commonsense r-cnn." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2020.

Therefore, the real-world problem may be simplified in this paper. More discussions of the limitations of the proposed approach are very helpful.

(3) (minor) The scope of the proposed work can be more precisely reflected in the paper (e.g., title). The title seems to be very general and broad. However, it is unclear how the proposed approach can be applied in other tasks (e.g., NLP), since it is unclear which is background and foreground in NLP.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The proposed solution has good intuitions. Overall the proposed approach seems to be solid, by following previous causal inference methods. The paper may simplify the real-world problems, and the assumptions made in the paper can be strong (as discussed in weakness (2)).

The paper is well written and easy to read. 

The main novelty of the paper is viewing an existing problem from a novel perspective (causal view). However, the paper seems to ignore some existing works. A discussion of the differences can be very helpful.

Yao, Yu, et al. "Instance-dependent label-noise learning under a structural causal model." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 4409-4420.
Wu, Songhua, et al. "Fair classification with instance-dependent label noise." Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning. PMLR, 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main novelty of the paper is viewing an existing problem from a novel perspective (causal view). However, the paper seems to ignore some existing works. A discussion of the differences will be very helpful. Besides, the paper seems to make strong assumptions that (i) the background and foreground is well defined and accurately known to the model and (ii) the confounders (in the proposed causal graph) are only from the background. However, in real-world images, the task can be more complex. For example, in images with complex scenes and multiple objects, the background and foreground may not be well-defined. And one object can be the confounder, when inference on the other object. More discussions of the limitations and scope of the work will be very helpful.
